transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-24 16:00 PT | Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Noah Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Cobalt Head of ML), Tom Reed (Cobalt SRE), Priya Shah (Cobalt Product), Ethan Cole (Cobalt DevOps)

Summary:
- Kickoff to define POC success criteria for latency/throughput (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing, and an initial measurement plan.
- Agreement to collect representative traces and run a hands-on benchmark early December.
- Action items: Redwood to produce benchmark matrix; Cobalt to share traffic samples and infra constraints.

Topics:
- Clarify TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (total per-token) SLO intent
- Define target percentiles (p95/p99) and acceptable tails
- Workload composition (short Q&A vs long generation) and sampling plan
- Measurement harness, environment (hosted vs dedicated vs private) and cost/runtime tradeoffs
- Security and on-prem constraints for routing/fallback

00:00 Maya: "All right, folks, thanks for joining. I'll give a quick agenda: scope success criteria, figure out the workload mix, set p95/p99 goals for TTFT and TPOT, and then align on next steps. Diego will walk the benchmark approach."
00:28 Lena: "Sounds good. For context, our app is a clinical summarization assistant. Mixed traffic — about 70% short requests (single-paragraph summaries), 30% long notes generation, and occasional batch embeddings. Latency is user-visible for triage flows."
00:45 Tom: "We also have constraints on PII handling and a private VPC requirement for any pilot that touches PHI. We'll try to keep data anonymized for the initial run, but we need to know if Redwood can support a VPC or on-prem path later."
01:10 Diego: "Understood. For the POC we can run in Redwood hosted infra with sanitized traces; after we validate SLOs we can move to Dedicated or Private. Quick question: is the primacy TTFT — i.e., time to first token for a user-facing typing experience — or TPOT/cost per token?"
01:31 Priya: "TTFT is most important for the triage UI — users expect answers quickly. For nightly batch jobs, TPOT and cost matter more. We need both, but TTFT gets top priority for acceptance."
02:05 Noah: "Just to set terms: TTFT is time-to-first-token (measured at the API ingress to the first byte returned). TPOT we'll treat as total per-token latency (or the wallclock to stream the entire response) — and we'll also report per-token throughput (tokens/sec)."
02:28 Lena: "Can we align on percentiles? We're thinking p95 for TTFT should be 150-200ms, p99 under 400ms for short prompts. Is that realistic?"
02:45 Diego: "Depends on model, sequence length, and batching. For a 7B quantized model on a dedicated GPU pool, p95 TTFT ~80-120ms is achievable; p99 can spike higher. On hosted multi-tenant we typically budget higher. For long generations TPOT p95 is more like 200-600ms per k tokens depending on context. We should map targets per workload class."
03:10 Tom: "We can't accept p99 > 1s on our triage flow. That will look bad to clinicians."
03:20 Maya: "Okay, let's capture hard acceptance criteria vs stretch goals. How about we propose: triage short (<=64 tokens) TTFT p95 <= 200ms, p99 <= 450ms as acceptance; stretch p95 <= 120ms p99 <= 300ms. Long generation (<=1024 tokens) TPOT p95 <= 1.2s per 100 tokens, p99 <= 2.5s per 100 tokens? We can iterate."
03:55 Priya: "The per-100-token metric is fine, we just need a consistent normalization. We'll model costs against TPOT eventually."
04:10 Diego: "Great. For benchmarking we recommend a matrix: workload class (short/medium/long), token distributions, concurrency levels, cold vs warm cache, routing fallback scenarios, and sample percentiles (p50/p95/p99/stddev). We'll also capture throughput (tokens/sec) at steady state."
04:40 Lena: "What about KV cache / prefix reuse? Our triage uses common prompt prefixes and we expect cache hits to reduce TTFT. Should we simulate different hit rates?"
04:55 Diego: "Yes — include cache hit tiers: 0%, 50%, 90% to show impact. Redwood supports prefix / KV caching. We'll instrument the runs to show delta. Also show batching effects at various concurrency points."
05:20 Ethan: "One constraint: our test environment has egress bandwidth caps and no GPU bursting for the private option. We'll document that so the benchmark matches realistic constraints."
05:40 Maya: "We'll need those infra details — Tom/Ethan can supply them. Next, measurement harness: we can provide a reproducible test runner (locally-run load runner + Redwood benchmark harness) and a template for traffic replay. Does that work?"
06:00 Tom: "Yes. We'll need instructions to anonymize PHI. Also, we may prefer to run the final acceptance benchmark in our staging VPC with Redwood Private if the hosted results are promising."
06:20 Diego: "That's fine. For the POC we'll do a two-phase run: 1) Redwood-hosted synthetic + sanitized trace replay to validate SLOs and tune config; 2) Staging replay in the customer's VPC/Private to validate network and egress behavior. Phase 2 only after we lock configs and sanity metrics."
06:45 Priya: "Timeline? We want results before end of Q4. Is that realistic?"
07:00 Maya: "If we get traces by Dec 1, Redwood can run phase 1 during the week of Dec 6 and share a results deck by Dec 10. Phase 2 (staging) could be the following week if needed. So timeline is tight but feasible."
07:20 Lena: "OK. Can you walk through an example benchmark plan now — what we'll see in the spreadsheet?"
07:35 Diego: "We'll have rows for workload class, sample prompt, median tokens, token variance, cache hit rate, concurrency sweep (1, 5, 10, 25, 50), ramp duration, measurement window, and steady-state token/sec. Columns for metrics: TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens estimate, and notes (warm vs cold)."
08:10 Noah: "We'll also capture error rates, HTTP 429/5xx counts, GPU utilization, and token generation variance. That helps correlate tail latency with resource saturation."
08:35 Tom: "A question on measuring TTFT — do you measure from our load generator to first byte or from Redwood's ingress?"
08:48 Diego: "We instrument both. We'll ask you to run the client-side replay (local to your VPC) and Redwood will log server-side ingress timestamps. We diff them to show network vs server latency. For acceptance we use server-side ingress to first byte to avoid network noise, but we'll show both."
09:10 Priya: "How do we handle model fallbacks? If the primary model can't meet latency, can we route to a smaller quantized variant?"
09:22 Maya: "Yes — Redwood supports routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible variants. We'll include a scenario where we intentionally constrain capacity to trigger fallback and measure user-visible TTFT impact."
09:45 Lena: "Cost tradeoff: we'd like suggestions — quantization, batching, dedicated capacity vs hosted. Can Redwood provide a recommended config for our workload mix?"
09:58 Diego: "Absolutely. After baseline runs we'll produce a recommendation sheet: model family + quantization level + batching target + caching policy + estimated cost per 1M tokens and latency profile."
10:20 Tom: "On the security side: SOC2 docs and SSO integration are gating items. We need to know if Redwood can do SAML SSO and KMS integration for private deployments."
10:35 Maya: "Yes — Redwood supports SAML, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations for Private. I'll send the security pack after the call. For hosted during the pilot we'll use sanitized data and limit retention as agreed."
10:52 Ethan: "Also want to flag that our compliance team requires audit logs at the request level for any run we do in production-like environments."
11:05 Noah: "We can enable request-level audit logs in Private and Dedicated; in hosted we'll provide request sampling and enhanced logs for the pilot. We'll document retention and access controls."
11:25 Priya: "One more: sample size for p99 — how much traffic do you need?"
11:33 Diego: "To get stable p99 estimates we prefer at least 10k requests per workload class during the steady window. If that's not feasible, we run more iterations and bootstrap confidence intervals. We'll also show running tails across multiple runs."
12:00 Lena: "Ok that's helpful. Anything else we should capture?"
12:08 Maya: "Recap: Acceptance criteria proposal — triage short TTFT p95 <= 200ms p99 <= 450ms; stretch p95 <= 120ms p99 <= 300ms. Long gen TPOT per-100-token p95 <= 1.2s p99 <= 2.5s. We'll formalize in the benchmark spreadsheet. Actions: Diego will draft benchmark matrix; Lena will provide traces; Maya will send security docs and pricing ballpark."
12:45 Tom: "Agree. We'll try to get the traces to you by Dec 1 and flag any network/egress limits in the same payload."
12:55 Maya: "Great. We'll set the hands-on slot for Dec 6. I'll send calendar invite and the benchmark template. Thanks everyone."

End of transcript.

Notes: Transcript contains minor transcription errors and speaker timing approximations typical of automated call capture. References: "TTFT" (time-to-first-token), "TPOT" (total per-token/time per token metric), KV cache/prefix cache, VPC/private deployment, SOC2/KMS, p95/p99 target discussion.
